events.title: Mir Qasim made Nawab of Bengal
events.summary: In October 1760 the Company removed Mir Jafar and made his son-in-law Mir Qasim Nawab of Bengal.
events.detail:
Mir Jafar could not pay the Company what he had promised, and he protested when it kept demanding more (NCERT). Governor Vansittart struck a deal with Mir Qasim, who paid for the throne with land and money.

Mir Qasim was able. He moved his capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr, trained an army in the European style and set his finances right. When Company servants kept misusing dastaks, he abolished internal duties for everyone. The Company saw this as defiance, and war broke out in 1763.

participants.role: Bought the throne, then tried to rule independently; moved his capital to Monghyr.
Deposed because he could not, or would not, pay what the Company demanded.
Governor of Bengal who deposed Mir Jafar and installed Mir Qasim.

facts: Mir Qasim shifted the capital of Bengal from Murshidabad to Monghyr.
He abolished internal duties for all traders so the Company lost its unfair advantage.
When he complained, he was defeated at Buxar (1764) and driven out of Bengal (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2 "From Trade to Territory" and Ch. 3 "Ruling the Countryside"; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3

events.yearHook: Mir Qasim takes the throne in 1760, the same year the French lose at Wandiwash.

events.title: Treaty of Allahabad: the Company gets the Diwani
events.summary: On 12 August 1765 the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II made the East India Company the Diwan of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
events.detail:
After Buxar the three defeated powers had to make peace. Clive came back to Bengal as Governor in May 1765 and signed two treaties at Allahabad.

The first, with **Shah Alam II** (12 August 1765), gave the Company the **Diwani** — the right to collect the land revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The second, with **Shuja-ud-Daula** (16 August 1765), gave Awadh back to its nawab. Clive did not annex Awadh: he wanted it as a buffer between Bengal and the Marathas and Afghans.
outcomes: The Company became the Diwan of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa — the start of its rule as a territorial power.
Clive set up the Dual Government in Bengal (1765–72).
Awadh became a buffer state between Company territory and the Marathas.

participants.role: Negotiated and signed both treaties.
Granted the Diwani by a farman in return for money and land.
Got Awadh back by paying the indemnity and giving up two districts.
His death in early 1765 left the Company free to set new terms in Bengal.
One of the three rulers defeated at Buxar; he got nothing and died in exile.

facts: On 12 August 1765 the Mughal emperor appointed the East India Company as the Diwan of Bengal (NCERT).

After the Diwani, the outflow of gold from Britain to India stopped (NCERT).
Two treaties were signed at Allahabad in 1765 — one with Shah Alam II, one with Shuja-ud-Daula.

The Company paid the emperor Rs 26 lakh a year.

events.yearHook: The year after Buxar: 1764 → 1765.

events.title: Dual Government in Bengal
events.summary: From 1765 to 1772 the Company held Bengal's revenue and army, while the Nawab held the blame for running the state.
events.detail:
Clive did not want the Company to rule Bengal openly — it would alarm other European powers and the British Parliament. So power was split. The Company held the **Diwani** (revenue) and the army. The Nawab kept the **Nizamat** (police and justice), but a deputy chosen by the Company ran it, and the Nawab got only a pension.

Indian deputies collected the revenue for the Company: Muhammad Reza Khan in Bengal and Raja Shitab Rai in Bihar. The Company had power without responsibility; the Nawab had responsibility without power.

participants.role: Designed the Dual Government.
Nawab in name only; let a Company-chosen deputy run the government.
His death in 1765 let the Company set new terms with his young son.
Ended the system in 1772 and took direct charge.

facts: Under Dual Government the Company had power without responsibility.
Ended by Warren Hastings in 1772; the treasury moved from Murshidabad to Calcutta.

alsoOn.text: Warren Hastings ends the Dual Government and moves the treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
causes: The Company had just got the Diwani (1765) but was not ready to rule openly.
Clive feared opposition from other Europeans and from Parliament if the Company took over.
Mir Jafar died in 1765; his young son Najm-ud-Daula could be made to accept any terms.
course: February 1765: Najm-ud-Daula agrees to let a Company-chosen deputy (Naib Subahdar) run the Nizamat.
August 1765: the Diwani is granted to the Company.
Revenue is collected through Indian deputy diwans, while Company servants enrich themselves.
1770: the great famine strikes Bengal.
1772: the Company "stands forth as Diwan" — Warren Hastings ends the system.

treaties.name: Treaty with Najm-ud-Daula
terms: The Nawab gave up control of the army and finances.
A deputy chosen by the Company ran the Nizamat.

gains: Company: Bengal's revenue without the duty of governing.
losses: Peasants and artisans: heavy revenue demands, decline of crafts and farming (NCERT).
outcomes: Misrule and suffering, made worse by the famine of 1770.

events.yearHook: Starts with the Diwani (1765), ends with Hastings (1772) — 7 years.

events.title: First Anglo-Mysore War
events.summary: Haidar Ali fights the Company, the Nizam and the Marathas — and wins.
events.detail:
Haidar Ali's growing power alarmed the Company in Madras. In 1767 war broke out. Haidar beat the British and reached close to Madras.

The war ended with the Treaty of Madras (1769): both sides returned conquered lands and promised to help each other if attacked.
events.place: Mysore and the Carnatic, up to Madras
outcomes: When the Marathas attacked Mysore in 1771, the Company did not help — breaking the treaty and causing the next war.

participants.role: Split the alliance against him, beat the British and dictated peace near Madras.
Switched sides twice — first to Haidar, then back to the Company.

facts: The four Anglo-Mysore wars: 1767–69, 1780–84, 1790–92 and 1799.
The First war ended with the Treaty of Madras (1769).

pairs.left: Haidar Ali at the gates of Madras

alsoOn.text: Treaty of Madras ends the First Anglo-Mysore War on Haidar Ali's terms.
The Marathas attack Mysore; the Company does not help Haidar Ali.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2 "From Trade to Territory"
causes: Haidar Ali had made Mysore a strong military state and was expanding.
By the Treaty of Hyderabad (1766) the Company promised the Nizam troops — against Haidar.
The Company, the Nizam and the Marathas formed a front against Mysore.
course: 1767: Haidar bribes the Marathas to withdraw and wins the Nizam over to his side.
1768: the Nizam makes peace with the Company again, leaving Haidar alone.
Haidar fights on, recovers his lost forts, and in 1769 rides to within a few miles of Madras.
4 April 1769: the frightened Madras council signs peace on Haidar's terms.

treaties.name: Treaty of Madras
terms: Both sides returned each other's conquests.
Each promised to help the other if attacked by a third power.

gains: Haidar Ali: won the war and great prestige.
losses: Company: lost face; the Madras council was humiliated.
events.yearHook: Mysore wars start 10 years after Plassey: 1757 + 10 = 1767.

events.title: Great Bengal Famine
events.summary: About one-third of Bengal's people die in a terrible famine.
events.detail:
Bengal's farmers were already squeezed by revenue demands under the Dual Government. Artisans had left their villages and farming showed signs of collapse (NCERT). When the rains failed in 1769, nothing was done to help.

In 1770 a terrible famine killed ten million people in Bengal — about one-third of the population (NCERT).
outcomes: Showed the failure of the Dual Government.
Revenue fell sharply, pushing the Company to reform revenue collection (1772) and, finally, to the Permanent Settlement (1793).
facts: In 1770 a terrible famine killed ten million people in Bengal; about one-third of the population was wiped out (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 3 "Ruling the Countryside"
causes: Failure of the monsoon in 1769.
Revenue was collected harshly even in the famine years.
Under the Dual Government no one took responsibility for relief.
losses: About ten million people died — one-third of Bengal's population (NCERT).
About a third of the cultivated land went out of use.
events.yearHook: A round year: 1770 — and 10 million dead.

events.title: First Anglo-Maratha War
events.summary: The Company backs Raghunathrao for Peshwa and gets drawn into a war with no clear winner.
events.detail:
After the murder of Peshwa Narayanrao (1773), Raghunathrao sought British help to become Peshwa (Treaty of Surat, 1775). The Maratha council led by Nana Phadnis fought back.

After years of fighting, the Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the war with no clear victor.

Peshwa whose murder (1773) began the succession crisis.
The baby Peshwa in whose name the Marathas fought.
Led the regency and the war against the British-backed Raghunathrao.
Main Maratha general in the north; later negotiated peace.
Governor-General who directed the war from Calcutta.

Defeated Mahadji Sindhia at Sipri (1781).

facts: Started by the Treaty of Surat (1775) with Raghunathrao.

A Company army surrendered at Wadgaon (1779).
Ended by the Treaty of Salbai (1782) with no clear victor (NCERT).

events.title: Second Anglo-Mysore War
events.summary: Haidar Ali, and then Tipu, fight the Company in the Carnatic.
events.detail:
Haidar Ali invaded the Carnatic in 1780 and won early victories. He died in 1782 and Tipu Sultan carried on the war.

It ended with the Treaty of Mangalore (1784): both sides returned each other's lands.
signatories: Lord Macartney, Governor of Madras (Treaty of Mangalore)
outcomes: A stalemate; the Company learnt that Mysore was its most dangerous enemy in the south.

Sent from Bengal; defeated Haidar at Porto Novo (1781).
Led the Madras army; retreated after Pollilur (1780).
Governor of Madras; signed the Treaty of Mangalore with Tipu.
Governor-General who sent men and money and split the enemy league.

facts: Haidar Ali died in 1782 during this war.

alsoOn.text: Treaty of Mangalore ends the Second Anglo-Mysore War.

sides.ruler: Haidar Ali, then Tipu Sultan (from December 1782)

events.title: Treaty of Salbai
events.summary: Signed on 17 May 1782, the Treaty of Salbai ended the First Anglo-Maratha War with no clear winner (NCERT) and gave 20 years of peace.
events.detail:
The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) began when the Bombay government backed Raghunathrao's claim to be Peshwa. It went badly for the Company: a Bombay army surrendered at Wadgaon (1779). Hastings sent armies from Bengal, which captured Gwalior (1780) and beat Mahadji Sindhia at Sipri (1781).

Both sides were tired. The Company also had to fight Haidar Ali in the south. Mahadji Sindhia acted as mediator and signed the treaty at Salbai, near Gwalior. Nana Phadnis ratified it for the Peshwa in 1783.
outcomes: No clear victor (NCERT).
About 20 years of peace between the Company and the Marathas — until the Treaty of Bassein (1802).
Mahadji Sindhia became the most powerful Maratha chief in the north.

participants.role: Negotiated and signed the treaty and stood guarantor for both sides.
Governor-General who wanted peace; his agent David Anderson signed.
Ran the Peshwa's government; ratified the treaty in 1783.
The child Peshwa whom the treaty recognised.
The Company's former ally; dropped by the treaty and pensioned.
Negotiated and signed the treaty for Hastings.
His capture of Gwalior (1780) put pressure on the Marathas.
His victory over Mahadji at Sipri (1781) pushed Mahadji to make peace.
Not a party; the Marathas promised to make him return the lands he had taken in the Carnatic.

facts: The First Anglo-Maratha War ended in 1782 with the Treaty of Salbai; there was no clear victor (NCERT).

events.yearHook: Haidar Ali dies the same year — 1782.

events.title: Pitt's India Act
events.summary: Creates a Board of Control in Britain over the Company.
events.detail:
The Regulating Act had not worked well. Pitt's India Act set up a Board of Control in London to direct the Company's political affairs, while the Court of Directors kept trade.

This 'dual control' lasted until 1858.

participants.role: British Prime Minister who passed the Act.
Governor-General when the Act was passed.

outcomes: Board of Control (6 members) supervised civil, military and revenue matters.
Company territories called 'British possessions in India' for the first time.
facts: Named after British PM William Pitt the Younger.
Set up dual control: Board of Control (politics) and Court of Directors (trade).
events.source: Standard constitutional history
causes: Under the Regulating Act the Governor-General could be outvoted by his council.
The Supreme Court and the council quarrelled over their powers.
Fox's India Bill (1783) to take over the Company failed in Parliament.
course: 1784: Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger passes the India Act.
A Board of Control of six members is set up in London to direct political, military and revenue affairs.
The Court of Directors keeps charge of trade and appointments.
The Governor-General's council is cut to three members, so he is harder to outvote.
Bombay and Madras are made fully subordinate to the Governor-General in war, diplomacy and revenue.
gains: The British government: real control over the Company's rule in India.
The Governor-General: more power over his council and the presidencies.
losses: The Company: its political independence.
events.yearHook: 1784 = three things: Pitt's Act, Asiatic Society, Treaty of Mangalore.

events.title: Asiatic Society of Bengal founded
events.summary: William Jones founds a society to study India's languages, laws and history.
events.detail:
William Jones, a judge of the Supreme Court in Calcutta, founded the Asiatic Society on 15 January 1784, with the support of Warren Hastings.

It began the journal Asiatick Researches and led the 'Orientalist' study of Sanskrit and Persian texts.

Governor-General who supported it.

Its journal was Asiatick Researches.
Warren Hastings also founded the Calcutta Madrasa (1781) to study Arabic, Persian and Islamic law.

Charles Wilkins translates the Bhagavad Gita into English.
Jonathan Duncan starts the Sanskrit College at Benaras.

causes: Some officials, called Orientalists, believed the British should learn Indian languages, laws and texts to rule well (NCERT).

events.title: Third Anglo-Mysore War
events.summary: Cornwallis, the Marathas and the Nizam defeat Tipu.
events.detail:
Tipu attacked Travancore, a British ally, in 1789. Cornwallis led the Company in alliance with the Marathas and the Nizam.

The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) forced Tipu to give up about half his kingdom and pay a huge indemnity. Two of his sons were taken as hostages.

outcomes: Mysore survived but could no longer threaten the Company alone.

events.summary: Renews the Company's trade monopoly for 20 years.
events.detail: The Company's charter was renewed for 20 more years. The powers of the Governor-General over Bombay and Madras were increased, and the salaries of the Board of Control were to be paid from Indian revenue.

causes: The Company's charter of trade had to be renewed by Parliament every 20 years.

events.title: Battle of Kharda
events.summary: The Marathas defeat the Nizam; the Company stays out.
events.detail:
The Marathas defeated Nizam Ali Khan at Kharda. Governor-General John Shore followed non-intervention and did not help the Nizam.

The Nizam then hired French officers for his army — one reason Wellesley later pushed him into the Subsidiary Alliance.

participants.role: Defeated and forced to cede land and pay an indemnity.
Ran the Maratha government that won the battle.
The Peshwa in whose name the war was fought.
Governor-General who did not intervene.

facts: The last occasion on which the Maratha chiefs fought together.
events.source: Standard modern Indian history

sides.name: Marathas
sides.ruler: Peshwa Madhavrao II (government of Nana Phadnis)

causes: The Marathas demanded arrears of chauth and sardeshmukhi from the Nizam.
The Nizam refused and hoped the British would help him.
course: March 1795: the armies meet at Kharda.
The Nizam is defeated and forced to sign a treaty.
Governor-General John Shore follows non-intervention and does not help.

treaties.name: Treaty of Kharda
terms: The Nizam ceded territory to the Marathas.
He paid a large war indemnity.

losses: Nizam: land and money; he felt let down by the British.
gains: Marathas: their last great joint victory.
outcomes: The Nizam hired French officers for his army.
This pushed Wellesley to bring him into the Subsidiary Alliance (1798).
events.yearHook: Halfway through the 1790s (1795) — the last time the Maratha chiefs fought together.

events.title: Ceded Districts: Rayalaseema passes to the Company
events.summary: The Nizam gives up the Rayalaseema districts to pay for the subsidiary force.
events.detail:
Under the Subsidiary Alliance the Nizam had to pay for British troops. In 1800 he gave up the districts he had gained from Mysore — Bellary, Cuddapah, Kurnool (part) and the Anantapur area — instead of cash.

They were called the 'Ceded Districts' and later became Rayalaseema. Thomas Munro was their first Principal Collector (1800–07).

participants.role: Ceded the districts.
First Principal Collector; introduced ryotwari here.
Governor-General who imposed the terms.

outcomes: Rayalaseema joined the Madras Presidency.
With the Northern Circars, almost all of present-day Andhra Pradesh came under the Company.
facts: 'Rayalaseema' (land of the Rayas) was a name adopted much later, in 1928.
Thomas Munro tried the ryotwari system in the Ceded Districts.
Sir Thomas Munro was the first Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.source: Standard Andhra history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: The Nizam had to pay for a larger subsidiary force after 1798.
Instead of cash, the Company asked for the lands he had gained from Mysore in 1792 and 1799.
course: 12 October 1800: a new subsidiary treaty is signed.
The Nizam hands over the districts.
Thomas Munro becomes Principal Collector (1800–07) and introduces ryotwari.

treaties.name: Subsidiary Treaty of 1800
terms: The Nizam ceded the districts he had got from Mysore — Bellary, Cuddapah, Kurnool (part) and the Anantapur area.
In return the Company maintained the enlarged subsidiary force.

gains: Company: all of Rayalaseema.
losses: Nizam: his share of Tipu's lands.
events.yearHook: The first year of 1800: Rayalaseema comes to the Company.

events.title: Fort William College, Calcutta
events.summary: Wellesley sets up a college to train Company officials in Indian languages.
events.detail:
Lord Wellesley founded Fort William College to teach young British officials Indian languages, laws and customs.

It also became a centre for writing and printing textbooks in Indian languages.

participants.role: Founded the college.

facts: Founded by Lord Wellesley in 1800.
events.source: Standard modern Indian history
causes: Wellesley believed young British officials knew too little about India to govern it.
course: 1800: Fort William College opens in Calcutta.
It teaches Indian languages, laws, history and customs.
It also produces grammars and textbooks in Indian languages, printed at the Serampore press.
outcomes: The Court of Directors disliked the cost; from 1806 training moved to Haileybury College in England.
events.yearHook: Founded in 1800, the first year of the new century.

events.title: Treaty of Bassein
events.summary: Peshwa Baji Rao II accepts the Subsidiary Alliance.
events.detail:
Defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar, Peshwa Baji Rao II fled to the British and signed the Treaty of Bassein on 31 December 1802, accepting a subsidiary force.

The other Maratha chiefs saw it as a surrender of Maratha independence, which led to the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
outcomes: The Peshwa became a subsidiary ally.
Triggered the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05).

participants.role: Signed away Maratha independence to regain his throne.
Governor-General who imposed it.
Defeated the Peshwa near Poona, so Baji Rao II fled to the British.
Escorted the Peshwa back to Poona (1803).
His death in 1800 left the Maratha state without a leader.
Defeated with the Peshwa near Poona; opposed the treaty.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history
causes: Nana Phadnis died in 1800, and the Maratha chiefs fought each other.
October 1802: Yashwantrao Holkar defeated the Peshwa and Sindhia near Poona.
Baji Rao II fled to Bassein and asked the British for help.
course: 31 December 1802: Baji Rao II signs the Treaty of Bassein.
May 1803: Arthur Wellesley escorts him back to Poona.
Sindhia and Bhonsle see it as the end of Maratha independence and prepare for war.

treaties.name: Treaty of Bassein
terms: The Peshwa accepted a subsidiary force of 6,000 troops.
He ceded territory to pay for it.
He would not employ other Europeans.
His dealings with other states would go through the Company.

gains: Company: control of the head of the Maratha confederacy.
Baji Rao II: his throne back.
losses: The Marathas: the Peshwa's independence.
events.yearHook: One year before the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803).

events.title: Second Anglo-Maratha War
events.summary: The Company defeats Sindhia and Bhonsle and takes Delhi and Agra.
events.detail:
Sindhia, Bhonsle and Holkar refused to accept the Treaty of Bassein. The war was fought on different fronts — Arthur Wellesley won at Assaye (1803) and General Lake at Laswari (1803).

The British gained Orissa and the territories north of the Yamuna, including Agra and Delhi. The Mughal emperor came under British protection.
outcomes: British gained Orissa and the land north of the Yamuna, including Agra and Delhi (NCERT).
Treaties: Deogaon (Bhonsle, 1803), Surji-Arjangaon (Sindhia, 1803), Rajpurghat (Holkar, 1805).

participants.role: Governor-General who fought the war; recalled in 1805.
Won the Battle of Assaye (1803).
Took Delhi and won at Laswari (1803).
Lost at Assaye and Laswari; signed Surji-Arjangaon.
Lost at Assaye and Argaon; signed Deogaon.
Fought the Company in 1804–05; made peace at Rajpurghat (1805).
Mughal emperor who passed into British protection at Delhi.
Sent back in 1805 to make peace; died at Ghazipur the same year.

facts: Battle of Assaye (1803) — won by Arthur Wellesley, later Duke of Wellington.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2 "From Trade to Territory"

sides.name: Maratha chiefs
sides.ruler: Daulat Rao Sindhia and Raghuji Bhonsle II (Holkar from 1804)

causes: Sindhia and Bhonsle refused to accept the Treaty of Bassein (1802).
Wellesley wanted to finish Maratha power in the north and take Delhi.
course: August 1803: war begins; Arthur Wellesley takes Ahmednagar.
September 1803: Lake takes Aligarh and Delhi; the Mughal emperor comes under British protection.
23 September 1803: Arthur Wellesley wins at Assaye.
1 November 1803: Lake wins at Laswari.
December 1803: Bhonsle and Sindhia make peace.
1804–05: Holkar fights on; he defeats Colonel Monson, and Lake fails to take Bharatpur.
1805: Wellesley is recalled for spending too much on wars; peace with Holkar at Rajpurghat.

treaties.name: Treaty of Deogaon
terms: Bhonsle gave up Cuttack (Orissa) and western Berar.
He accepted a British Resident.

treaties.name: Treaty of Surji-Arjangaon
terms: Sindhia gave up his lands between the Ganga and the Yamuna, and Ahmednagar and Broach.
He gave up control of the Mughal emperor.

treaties.name: Treaty of Rajpurghat
terms: Holkar gave up claims north of the Chambal.
He kept most of his own lands.

losses: Marathas: Orissa, the Doab, Delhi and Agra.
Company: heavy costs; defeat of Monson and failure at Bharatpur.
gains: Company: Orissa and the land north of the Yamuna, including Agra and Delhi (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Wellesley is recalled; Cornwallis returns as Governor-General and dies at Ghazipur.

events.yearHook: 1803–05: it ends the same year Wellesley leaves India (1805).

events.title: Battle of Wandiwash: the French are beaten
events.summary: Eyre Coote defeats Count de Lally at Wandiwash on 22 January 1760 — the end of the French challenge in India.
events.detail:
The English and the French fought three Carnatic Wars for control of south India. In the third (1756–63), part of the Seven Years' War in Europe, the French under Count de Lally attacked Madras but failed.

At Wandiwash in the Carnatic, Eyre Coote crushed Lally's army. Pondicherry fell a year later. The Treaty of Paris (1763) gave the French back their trading posts, but they could never again be a military power in India.
causes: Anglo-French rivalry for trade and power in south India (the Carnatic Wars).
The Seven Years' War (1756–63) in Europe set Britain and France at war again.
Lally besieged Madras (1758–59) and recalled Bussy from Hyderabad, weakening the French hold on the Deccan.
course: 1758: Lally arrives and captures Fort St David.
1759: his siege of Madras fails; the British take Masulipatnam.
22 January 1760: Eyre Coote defeats Lally at Wandiwash; Bussy is taken prisoner.
January 1761: Pondicherry surrenders to the British.

treaties.name: Treaty of Paris
terms: Ended the Seven Years' War.
Pondicherry and other French factories in India were returned.
The French could not fortify them or keep troops in Bengal.

losses: French: their army in India, Pondicherry (till 1763) and all political influence.
gains: English: no European rival left in India.
outcomes: The French remained only as traders in India.
Lally was executed in France (1766).

participants.role: Commanded the English army and won the battle.
French commander; lost the battle and later Pondicherry.
Recalled from Hyderabad; taken prisoner at Wandiwash.

facts: Battle of Wandiwash: 22 January 1760.
It decided the Anglo-French struggle in India — the Third Carnatic War (1756–63).
Treaty of Paris (1763) gave back the French factories but without forts or troops.

pairs.right: Eyre Coote vs Count de Lally
End of the Third Carnatic War

alsoOn.text: Pondicherry surrenders to the British.
Treaty of Paris ends the Seven Years' War; French factories in India returned without forts.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
events.yearHook: The French fall in 1760 — one year before the Marathas fall at Panipat (1761).

events.title: Treaty of Benares
events.summary: Warren Hastings sells Kora and Allahabad to Awadh and lends Company troops to Shuja-ud-Daula.
events.detail:
Shah Alam II left British protection in 1771 and went to Delhi with the Marathas. Hastings said he had broken the Treaty of Allahabad, stopped his Rs 26 lakh tribute, and took back Kora and Allahabad.

At Benares (September 1773) Hastings sold the two districts to Shuja-ud-Daula for Rs 50 lakh and agreed to lend him Company troops, paid for by Shuja, against the Rohillas.
causes: Shah Alam II went over to the Marathas (1771), so Hastings stopped his tribute.
The Company needed money; Awadh would pay for the districts and for troops.
Hastings wanted a strong Awadh as a buffer against the Marathas.

treaties.name: Treaty of Benares
terms: Kora and Allahabad were sold to Awadh for Rs 50 lakh.
The Company would lend a brigade to Shuja, who paid for it.
The tribute of Rs 26 lakh to Shah Alam II was stopped.

gains: Company: Rs 50 lakh and payment for its troops.
Awadh: two districts and British military help.
losses: Shah Alam II: his tribute and his districts.
outcomes: Company troops helped Awadh conquer Rohilkhand (1774).
The Rohilla War became one of the charges against Hastings.

participants.role: Made the deal and stopped the emperor's tribute.
Bought Kora and Allahabad and hired Company troops.
Lost his tribute and districts after joining the Marathas.

facts: Treaty of Benares (1773): Kora and Allahabad sold to Awadh for Rs 50 lakh.
events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
events.yearHook: Same year as the Regulating Act — Hastings's first year in charge.

events.title: Rohilla War
events.summary: Company troops help the Nawab of Awadh conquer Rohilkhand.
events.detail: Under the Treaty of Benares, Company troops joined Shuja-ud-Daula against the Rohilla Afghans of Rohilkhand. At Miranpur Katra (April 1774) the Rohillas were defeated and their leader Hafiz Rahmat Khan was killed. Rohilkhand was added to Awadh.
causes: Shuja-ud-Daula claimed money the Rohillas had promised him for protection against the Marathas.
The Treaty of Benares gave him Company troops for the campaign.
losses: Rohillas: their leader killed and their land lost.
gains: Awadh: Rohilkhand.
outcomes: Critics said Hastings had hired out Company soldiers — a charge in his impeachment.

participants.role: Led the campaign and annexed Rohilkhand.
Lent the Company troops.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
events.yearHook: The year after Benares (1773 → 1774); the Supreme Court at Calcutta opened the same year.

events.title: Treaty of Faizabad
events.summary: The new Nawab of Awadh, Asaf-ud-Daula, gives Benares to the Company.
events.detail:
Shuja-ud-Daula died in January 1775. The Governor-General's council — then controlled by Hastings's opponents Philip Francis, Clavering and Monson — made a fresh treaty with his son Asaf-ud-Daula.

Asaf-ud-Daula gave the Company the zamindari of Benares (held by Raja Chait Singh) and agreed to pay more for the Company brigade in Awadh.

sides.name: East India Company
sides.ruler: Governor-General's council (majority led by Philip Francis)

causes: A new nawab gave the Company a chance to set new terms.
The council majority wanted more money and territory from Awadh.

treaties.name: Treaty of Faizabad
terms: Benares (Chait Singh's zamindari) passed to the Company.
Awadh paid more for the Company brigade.

gains: Company: Benares and more money.
losses: Awadh: Benares.
outcomes: Later quarrels over money led Hastings to depose Chait Singh and seize the treasure of the Begums of Awadh (1781).

participants.role: New nawab; gave up Benares.
Led the council majority that made the treaty.
Raja of Benares; came under the Company.
His death in January 1775 made the new treaty possible.
Governor-General, outvoted by his council at the time.

alsoOn.text: Hastings deposes Chait Singh of Benares and seizes the treasure of the Begums of Awadh — later charges in his impeachment.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
events.yearHook: Shuja-ud-Daula dies in 1775, so his son signs a new treaty the same year.

events.title: Treaty of Lucknow: Awadh cedes half its land
events.summary: Wellesley forces Saadat Ali Khan II to give over half of Awadh to the Company (NCERT).
events.detail: Awadh could not pay for the subsidiary force. Wellesley demanded land instead. In November 1801 the Nawab signed away Rohilkhand, Gorakhpur and the lower Doab — over half his territory (NCERT).
causes: Awadh failed to pay for the subsidiary force (NCERT).
Wellesley wanted Awadh's rich lands and a frontier against the Marathas and Afghans.

treaties.name: Treaty of Lucknow
terms: Awadh ceded Rohilkhand, Gorakhpur and the lower Doab to the Company.
In return the Company took over the cost of the subsidiary force.

gains: Company: over half of Awadh.
losses: Awadh: over half its territory (NCERT).

participants.role: Demanded the land.
Signed away half his kingdom.

facts: When Wellesley was Governor-General, Awadh was forced to give over half of its territory in 1801 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
events.yearHook: Hyderabad 1800, Awadh 1801, Peshwa 1802 — one a year.
outcomes: The Company gained Rohilkhand, the Doab and Gorakhpur — about half of Awadh.
Awadh became a weak buffer state until annexation (1856).

events.title: Battle of Bobbili
events.summary: In January 1757 the French under Bussy and the Raja of Vizianagaram, Vijayarama Raju, destroy Bobbili fort; its defenders die fighting and the women commit jauhar, and Tandra Paparayudu kills Vijayarama Raju in revenge.
events.detail:
The Northern Circars had been granted to the French (1753) to pay Bussy's troops. The rival zamindars of Bobbili (Velamas under Ranga Rao) and Vizianagaram (Pusapatis) fought for supremacy; Vijayarama Raju used Bussy against Bobbili. The story is told in the ballad "Bobbili Katha" and in Telugu films.

It shows the syllabus topic "Zamindary, Polegary System — Native States and Little Kings": hundreds of zamindars and poligars ruled in the Circars and Rayalaseema until the Company curbed them (Permanent Settlement 1802; Munro in the Ceded Districts).
causes: Rivalry of Bobbili and Vizianagaram zamindars.
French control of the Northern Circars (1753).
losses: Bobbili fort destroyed; defenders and women died.
outcomes: Vizianagaram became the leading zamindari of the north Circars.
The Circars passed to the English in 1765–66.
events.yearHook: January 1757 — six months before Plassey.

participants.role: French commander.
Raja of Vizianagaram; killed.
Killed Vijayarama Raju.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
